title: The injured child
subtitle: Weight first, blood early, scan selectively

sources.org: American College of Surgeons Committee on Trauma
sources.title: Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) Student Course Manual: paediatric trauma

sources.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
sources.title: Major trauma: assessment and initial management (NG39)

sources.org: Pediatric Emergency Care Applied Research Network (PECARN)
sources.title: Identification of children at very low risk of clinically-important brain injuries after head trauma (Kuppermann et al, Lancet 2009;374:1160-70)

sources.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
sources.title: Head injury: assessment and early management (NG232)

red_flags.text: Tachycardia, prolonged capillary refill, cool peripheries or altered behaviour. Children hold their blood pressure until very late; hypotension is a pre-arrest sign.
Abdominal bruising, a seat-belt sign or handlebar mark: a marker of visceral, pancreatic or bowel injury.
Reduced conscious level, a boggy scalp haematoma in an infant, or a full fontanelle.
An injury pattern that does not fit the history, delayed presentation, or injuries in a non-mobile infant: consider non-accidental injury.
Thoracic injury without rib fractures. The child's compliant chest wall transmits force to the lungs and heart without breaking.

do_now.text: Estimate weight immediately, from a parent-held record, a length-based tape or an age formula, and write it on the board. Every drug, fluid and tube size follows from it.
Airway with cervical spine protection, oxygen, and control of external haemorrhage. Infants' large occiput flexes the neck; pad under the shoulders.
Intravenous or intraosseous access without prolonged attempts. Intraosseous access is appropriate early in a shocked child.

Shock from haemorrhage: ATLS advises a single warmed isotonic crystalloid bolus of 20 mL/kg, then blood at 10 mL/kg if the child does not respond. NICE favours moving to blood components early and limiting crystalloid in active bleeding. Activate the paediatric major haemorrhage protocol.

Give tranexamic acid as soon as possible in a child with major trauma and active or suspected bleeding, at the weight-based dose in the local paediatric protocol, and not later than three hours after injury.

assess.text: Use age-specific vital sign ranges. A heart rate normal for an adult may be shock in a toddler.
Paediatric GCS, pupils and glucose. Record by component.
Apply the PECARN head rule for the child with a minor head injury and GCS 14 or 15 to decide between CT, observation and discharge.
Secondary survey with the child exposed but kept warm. Children lose heat fast and hypothermia worsens coagulopathy.

investigate.text: Blood gas, full blood count, coagulation, crossmatch, amylase or lipase and liver enzymes; urinalysis for haematuria.
Imaging selectively, not as a pan-scan by default: radiation matters more in children. CT the regions that the clinical findings and the mechanism direct.
CT head using NICE NG232 criteria for children, or the PECARN rule where it is the local standard. Neither applies to a child with a GCS below 14.
FAST is useful when positive in an unstable child but a negative FAST does not exclude solid organ injury.
Skeletal survey and safeguarding referral when non-accidental injury is a possibility.

resuscitate.text: Transfuse red cells and plasma together in active haemorrhage, with platelets and fibrinogen guided by the paediatric major haemorrhage protocol and point-of-care testing.
Maintain normothermia actively: warmed fluids, warm room, overhead heaters.
Gastric decompression with a nasogastric or orogastric tube. Crying children swallow air, and a distended stomach splints the diaphragm and mimics abdominal injury.
Weight-based analgesia early; a child in pain cannot be examined reliably.

definitive.text: Haemodynamically stable children with blunt splenic or liver injury: non-operative management in a unit with paediatric surgical and intensive care capacity is the standard.

Operate for haemodynamic instability despite blood transfusion, peritonitis, or hollow viscus injury. Transfusion need beyond the major haemorrhage threshold in a protocol is a surgical decision, not an observation one.
Surgically significant intracranial haematoma: neurosurgery without delay.

escalate.text: Paediatric major trauma centre for any severely injured child. Stabilise and transfer rather than undertaking non-essential procedures locally.
Paediatric anaesthetist and intensive care early, particularly for the airway.
Safeguarding team for any concern about the mechanism, the history or the timing.

notes: A child compensates for haemorrhage by tachycardia and vasoconstriction, then decompensates abruptly. Treat the trend, not a normal blood pressure.
Most paediatric solid organ injuries settle without surgery. The skill is selecting the few who do not, and being in a place that can operate when they declare themselves.
Write the weight, the fluid bolus volume and the blood volume on the board at the start. Arithmetic under pressure is where paediatric resuscitation goes wrong.
